title: TC0-07046

Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She appeals the RPD's decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).1 DETERMINATION The appeal is allowed.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of India who allegedly fears her brother-in-law and several other family members who support him. She also makes a sur place claim based on her support for the Khalistan movement since arriving in Canada. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denied her claim in a decision dated February 17, 2020, after finding that she lacks credibility and has an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai. She appeals the RPD's decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).1 DETERMINATION
The appeal is allowed. The matter is referred back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.2 SUMMARY OF THE FACTS

The Appellant is a 32-year-old woman from New Delhi who alleges that her brother-in-law was making inappropriate sexual advances and threatening her. She recounts a number of incidents in her Basis of Claim form (BOC), beginning several days after her sister's wedding on XXXX XXXX, 2010, up to XXXX XXXX, 2018, when her brother-in-law threatened her at gunpoint. Her mother and brother were assisting her brother-in-law, and even attended her home after she left India to inquire about her. She left India for Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, and filed her claim for refugee protection on September 9, 2018.

The Appellant also alleges that she developed an interest in the Khalistan movement after arriving in Canada, which seeks an independent Sikh state in Punjab, and became involved with the group "Sikhs for Justice" and their Sikh Referendum 2020 initiative.

The Appellant submits proposed new evidence which includes her father's identity card listing all family members, a family photograph with her brother-in-law, her registration to vote in the Khalistan Referendum 2020, numerous news articles on the Khalistan movement and the referendum, and several news articles on the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic in India.

New evidence is only admissible before the RAD if it arose after the rejection of the claims, if it was not reasonably available, or if the Appellant could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence at the time of the rejection of the claims.3 In addition to these legislative requirements, under the Federal Court of Appeal decisions in Singh and Raza, admissibility is limited to evidence that is relevant, new, and credible.4 [1] Regardless of whether the evidence meets the legislative and common law requirements, the question of its admissibility is moot because the appeal is granted without consideration of this evidence. None of this evidence would allow me to substitute my determination rather than refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.5 ISSUES

The issues on appeal are whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility, in its finding that she has a viable IFA in Mumbai, and whether it failed to consider her sur place claim.

The standard of correctness applies to this appeal as set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica.6 This requires an independent assessment of the refugee claim to determine whether the RPD was correct in its findings and determinations.7 While deference can be afforded to the RPD on specific issues when it enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, such an advantage does not arise in the present case.

After considering the Appellant's arguments and conducting an independent review of the record, which includes the transcript of the proceeding before the RPD, I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in its assessment of her credibility and failed to consider her sur place claim.

The RPD's adverse credibility findings are based primarily on the lack of documentary evidence establishing the identity of the agents of harm and the Appellant's family members, including their birth and marriage certificates. The RPD held that "without the aforementioned documentary evidence the claimant has not established persuasively that she has a sister called [...] and a brother called [...] as alleged and without a marriage certificate, the claimant has not established persuasively that [...] was her brother-in-law, married to her sister [...] as alleged. Therefore, the panel disbelieves that [...] lived in India and was the claimant's brother-in-law as alleged."

The RPD erred by impugning the Appellant's credibility based on the lack of corroborative evidence without first having a valid reason to question her credibility. The Federal Court succinctly explained the principle in Pooya: Going back to first principles, XXXX claimants are not required to provide XXXX XXXX unless there are valid reasons to question a claimant's credibility. This is because when a XXXX claimant swears the truth of certain allegations, there is a presumption that those allegations are true, unless there is reason to doubt their truthfulness (Maldonado v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1980] 2 FC 302 at para 5, [1979] FCJ No 248 (QL) (CA) [Maldonado]).8

In the present circumstances, the RPD cited the principle from Maldonado that sworn testimony is presumed to be true unless there is a valid reason to doubt its truthfulness, but incorrectly proceeded to impugn her testimony based on the lack of corroborative evidence without first having a reason to question her credibility.9 While the presumption of truthfulness can be rebutted, the RPD did not identify a reason to question the Appellant's credibility and "there is no general requirement for corroboration and a panel cannot make a credibility finding based on the absence of XXXX XXXX alone."10

The RPD also incorrectly impugned the Appellant's credibility and found that several letters and an affidavit were fraudulent because they did not include identity documents from the authors, and because the evidence in the National Documentation Package for India (NDP), indicates that certain documents can be manufactured.11 This is contrary to Federal Court jurisprudence that the prevalence of fraudulent documents in a claimant's home country is not a sufficient basis on its own to find that a document is fraudulent in the absence of evidence that brings its authenticity into question in the specific case.12

The RPD erred by failing to consider the Appellant's sur place claim and her alleged fear stemming from her activities in Canada on the Sikh Referendum 2020 initiative. This issue was expressly raised by the Appellant and her counsel during the hearing. Despite informing the Appellant that "I don't allow normally to do this, but I am allowing you to submit whatever other documents you wish to submit," the RPD did not address the sur place claim in its decision.

The Appellant submits that "she believed that her activities in which she took part at the Gurudwara (Sikh Temple) in Brampton, Ontario, came to the attention of the Indian authorities," although the RPD did not question her about whether her activities came to the attention of the authorities in India, and instead focused on the omission of the sur place claim from the BOC. The analytical framework for assessing a sur place claim was outlined by the Federal Court in Ngongo: "[t]he only relevant question is whether activities abroad might give rise to a negative reaction on the part of the authorities and thus a reasonable chance of persecution in the event of return."13 The analysis has been described as focusing "on whether the activities of an individual abroad might give rise to a negative reaction on the part of the authorities in their home country and lead to a reasonable chance of persecution in the event of return."14 Since the RPD did not question the Appellant on this issue, I cannot assess her credibility surrounding her alleged involvement in the Khalistan movement in Canada to determine whether her activities came to the attention of the Indian authorities.

Nor can I assess the viability of an IFA without first assessing the credibility of the Appellant's sur place claim. The Appellant's credibility surrounding her sur place claim and the question of whether her activities became known to the Indian authorities are central issues in the first part of the IFA analysis since they would determine whether the agents of harm include state actors.

I cannot substitute my own determination without a comprehensive assessment of the Appellant's credibility, including her sur place claim and the question of whether her alleged activities are known to the Indian authorities. A referral back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel is therefore the appropriate remedy in the circumstances.15 CONCLUSION

The appeal is allowed.
